title: Testing against brute force
objectives: Stress test a solution against a brute force on random cases.

screens.title: Test 7
screens.prose: Your fast solution to lesson 2's problem H passed all its examples. The judge disagrees. During a round Codeforces shows only the verdict, never the failing test.

lines: 3  H        Time limit exceeded on test 12
params.title: My submissions

screens.question: Tap the verdict that says the answer is wrong, not slow or crashed.

hints.text: Three verdicts mean three different failures.
*Time limit* means slow; *runtime error* means a crash.
Only *Wrong answer* says the program finished and printed something wrong.

feedback.correct: Wrong answer on test 7: the program ran in time and printed the wrong number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the verdict about the output itself.

byKey.l3: That says too slow. The answer might have been right.
byKey.l4: That says the program crashed before it answered.
byKey.l5: That submission was accepted, and it was for problem G.

explain.text: A wrong answer on a hidden test leaves you with no input to debug. So we make our own failing input, which is what this lesson builds.

screens.title: Make your own test 7
screens.prose: No test 7, so we make tests. A slow count that checks every pair, which we trust, runs beside the fast one on small random inputs. Step through the trials.
screens.question: On which trial do the two counts first disagree?

widget.accept: Trial 5: the fast count says 0 and the slow one 1.
widget.label: Trial

hints.text: Slide to the last trial.
Compare the last two columns on each row.
Rows 1 to 4 agree; on trial 5, `[4, 10, 2, 6, 1, 1]` with $k = 2$, fast says 0 and brute 1.

feedback.correct: Trial 5, a case six numbers long that we can check by hand.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first row where fast and brute differ.

byKey.four: Trial 4 agrees: both count 2. Look one row further.

explain.text: The two counts agree until trial 5. There $1 + 1 = 2 \le k = 2$, one pair, and the fast count missed it. Now we have a test 7 of our own, small enough to read.

screens.title: Stress testing
screens.prose: What you just watched is **stress testing**. A **brute force** you trust, slow but obviously correct, runs beside the fast code. A **generator** makes small random cases from a **seed**, and a loop compares the two.
screens.question: Put the lines of the stress loop in order.

hints.text: The seed is used once, before any trial.
Each trial makes a case, then compares.
Seed the generator, loop, make a case and compare. Return the case if they differ, and `None` if no trial did.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow one trial: make a case, then compare.

explain.text: Seeding once makes the run repeatable: the same seed gives the same cases. So a failure can always be found again. The loop stops at the first disagreement, which is the case we want to read.

screens.title: Which generator?
screens.prose: The bug is `<` where problem H needs `<=`. It shows only when a pair sums to exactly $k$. Two generators, both with $n$ from 1 to 6.

lines: gen A: values 1 to 10⁹, k from 2 to 2·10⁹
gen B: values 1 to 10,  k from 2 to 20
params.title: Two generators

screens.question: Which generator exposes the bug sooner?

options.text: B: small values make exact ties common
A: it covers the whole range of the constraints
options.why: You chose realism. With values up to $10^9$, a pair summing to exactly $k$ almost never happens.

options.text: Both equally: the bug is in every case
options.why: The bug changes the answer only when a pair sums to exactly $k$.

hints.text: When does `<` give a different count from `<=`?
Only when some $a_i + a_j = k$ exactly.
Exact ties are common with values up to 10 and vanishingly rare up to $10^9$.

feedback.correct: Small values make ties, and ties expose `<`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how often a pair sums to exactly $k$.

byKey.a: You chose the full range. Ties are then so rare that the bug hides.

explain.text: With seed 1, gen B found the bug on trial 5. Gen A found nothing in 100,000 trials on each of four seeds. Small ranges make the ties where this bug lives.

screens.title: Shrink the case
screens.prose: Trial 5 failed on `[4, 10, 2, 6, 1, 1]`, $k = 2$: fast 0, brute 1. A smaller failing case is easier to trace by hand.
screens.question: Which smaller case still makes the two counts differ?

options.why: No pair sums to at most 2 there, so both count 0.
One value has no pairs, so both count 0.
$1 + 1 = 2 < 3$, so the `<` version counts it too. Keep $k = 2$.

hints.text: Which pair did the fast count miss?
The only pair with sum at most 2 is $1 + 1$.
Keep the two 1s and $k = 2$; drop everything else.

feedback.correct: Two values and one pair: the bug in its smallest form.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the pair that sums to exactly $k$.

byKey.k3: You changed $k$. With $k = 3$ the pair's sum 2 is strictly less, so the bug does not show.

explain.text: On `[1, 1]` with $k = 2$ the fast count checks $1 + 1 < 2$, which is false. One line of tracing shows the `<`. Shrinking, by removing values while the counts still differ, takes a minute and saves many.

screens.title: A brute force with the same bug
screens.prose: Here the fast and slow versions share a helper. The stress test ran 100,000 trials and found no difference.

lines: def fast(xs, k): ...  # calls fits too
params.title: stress.py

screens.question: What does the clean run tell you?

options.text: Little: both call `fits`, so a bug there is in both
`fast` is correct on small cases
options.why: You trusted a brute force that shares the fast one's helper. If `fits` is wrong, both are wrong together.

options.text: The generator's cases are too small
options.why: Small cases are right for stress testing. The brute force is the problem.

hints.text: Is `brute` independent of `fast`?
Line 2 is used by both.
`fits` has the same `<` bug, and both versions inherit it, so they agree on every case.

feedback.correct: A brute force must share nothing with the fast code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the two versions have in common.

byKey.correct: You trusted the agreement. Both call `fits`, whose `<` is the bug, so they agree and are both wrong.

explain.text: Agreement proves only that the two versions match, and these share line 2's bug. Write the brute force from the statement alone, with the comparison spelled out: `xs[i] + xs[j] <= k`.

screens.title: The stress pattern

lines: Print any pair i < j with aᵢ + aⱼ = k,
If there are several answers, print any.
params.title: Problem G2

screens.question: For problem G2, how should the stress loop compare the two programs?

options.text: Check that fast's pair is valid, and that it says -1 only when brute finds none
`fast(case) != brute(case)`, as above
options.why: Two correct programs can print different pairs. Equality would report a bug that is not there.

options.text: Sort both answers, then compare them
options.why: Two different valid pairs stay different after sorting.

feedback.correct: With many valid answers, check the answer, not its equality.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two right answers may differ.

explain.text: When the statement says *print any*, the comparison becomes a **checker**: is fast's answer valid for this case? Level 3 meets such problems often.

screens.title: Write the stress loop
screens.prose: Write `stress(fast, brute, gen, trials, seed)`. Make one `random.Random(seed)` and call `gen(rng)` once per trial. Return the first case where the two differ, or `None`. Some fast functions sort their input in place, so give each function its own copy.

lines: fast_in_place(case) sorts xs in place first
params.title: Already defined

screens.question: Write `stress`.

widget.starter:
import copy
import random


def stress(fast, brute, gen, trials, seed):
    ...

tests.call: stress(lambda x: 0 if x == 13 else x, lambda x: x, lambda r: r.randint(0, 20), 1000, 2)
stress(fast_strict, brute_pairs, gen_pairs, 1000, 2) == stress(fast_strict, brute_pairs, gen_pairs, 1000, 2)

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests with the functions listed above, which are already defined. Test 9's fast function sorts its input in place; the case you return must be the one `gen` made. Answers are compared exactly.

hints.text: Make `rng` once, before the loop.
A sort inside `fast` changes the list it was given, and that is the list you would return.
For each trial: `case = gen(rng)`; compare `fast(copy.deepcopy(case))` with `brute(copy.deepcopy(case))`; return `case` on a difference. Return `None` after the loop.

feedback.correct: A seeded loop that returns the first disagreeing case, untouched.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-9: Test 9's fast function sorted the case before you returned it. Pass each function `copy.deepcopy(case)`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 allows only 4 trials, and the first failure is on trial 5. Run exactly `trials` trials.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects the trial-5 case for seed 1. Make one `random.Random(seed)` and call `gen` once per trial.
byKey.test-7: Test 7's cases are plain ints, not pairs. Pass the case to `fast` and `brute` as it is.

explain.text: One seeded generator makes the run repeatable, so seed 1 always fails on trial 5. Copying the case keeps what you return equal to what was tested. In a real contest you would print the case and stop.

screens.title: A stress test in pytest
screens.prose: Write `brute_pair_sums(xs, k)` straight from problem H's statement. Then write `test_against_brute()`. Its generator draws $n$ from 1 to 6, values from −5 to 5 and $k$ from −10 to 10. It asserts that `stress` finds no difference in 500 trials.

lines: n (1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵) values aᵢ and k
Count pairs i < j with aᵢ + aⱼ ≤ k.
params.title: Problem H

screens.question: Write `brute_pair_sums` and `test_against_brute`.

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 4 call your brute force. Test 5 runs your test on the correct `pair_sums_at_most`, where it must pass. Tests 6 to 10 each swap in a wrong one, where it must fail. Run examples runs pytest on your file.

hints.text: The brute force checks every pair $i < j$ with the statement's own `<=`.
Wrap the two functions so each takes one `case`: `lambda case: pair_sums_at_most(*case)`.
Define `gen(rng)` returning `(xs, k)`, then `assert stress(fast, brute, gen, 500, 1) is None` inside the test.

feedback.correct: A brute force from the statement, and a test that catches every planted bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 calls `brute_pair_sums([1, 2, 3], 4)` and expects 2: the pairs summing to 3 and 4.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 runs your test on the correct function and it failed. Check the brute force and the generator.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 swapped in a version with `<`, and your test passed it. Assert `is None`, and do not let `brute_pair_sums` call `pair_sums_at_most`.
byKey.test-10: Test 10's wrong version fails only when $k < 0$. Let your generator's $k$ go negative.

explain.text: The brute force shares nothing with the fast code, so it fails differently. The test then catches every planted bug, including one that shows only for negative $k$. Kept in the test file, it runs again after every change.

screens.title: Backtests and pricers
screens.prose: The same habit checks quant code. A vectorised backtest is fast and easy to get subtly wrong, often by one day. Run it against a slow loop on random short price paths, as the `backtest` course does in its first lesson.
screens.question: Which slow reference should the vectorised P&L be checked against?

options.text: A plain loop over days: yesterday's position times today's return
The same vectorised function on a shorter path
options.why: You compared the code with itself. It shares every bug, as the trap's helper did.

options.text: A closed form for random paths
options.why: A random path has no closed-form P&L. The loop written from the definition is the reference.

hints.text: The reference must be slow, obvious and independent.
It should follow the definition of P&L line by line.
Loop over the days; add yesterday's position times today's return. Then shrink trial 3 and trace it.

feedback.correct: An independent loop from the definition; then shrink trial 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the reference that shares no code with the fast version.

byKey.shorter: You chose the fast code again. Agreement with itself proves nothing.

explain.text: A loop from the definition is the brute force, and random short paths are the generator. Trial 3, prices £100, £98.50, £98, £99.25, £100.50, shows the vectorised code dropping the last day's £1.25. A fast option pricer is checked the same way, against Black-Scholes where a closed form exists.

ideas: Stress testing compares a fast solution with a slow, obviously correct brute force on many small random cases.
Seed the generator so failures repeat, keep $n$ and the values small so ties happen, then shrink the failing case.
The brute force must share no code with the fast solution, and many valid answers need a checker, not equality.

formula.name: The stress loop
formula.note: One seeded `random.Random(seed)` for the whole run.

summary.trap: A brute force that calls the fast solution's helper agrees with it on every case, bugs included.

quiz.prose: A stress test finds a failing case of 50,000 values.
quiz.question: What should you do next?

options.text: Generate small cases instead, with $n$ up to about 6, and find a failure you can read
Print the 50,000 values and study them
options.why: You chose to read a case far too large to trace by hand.

options.text: Submit again: the judge may disagree
options.why: The same code gives the same answer. Find the bug first.

feedback.correct: Small cases make the bug visible.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which case you can trace by hand.

explain.text: A failing case is useful only if you can trace it. Most bugs also show on tiny inputs, so a small generator finds one you can read in seconds.

quiz.prose: Your stress test printed *differ* and you closed the terminal before copying the case. You used `random.Random(4)`.
quiz.question: How do you get the case back?

options.text: Run it again with seed 4: the same seed makes the same cases
It is lost: random cases never repeat
options.why: You treated the cases as truly random. A seeded generator repeats them exactly.

options.text: Seed with the current time to cover more cases
options.why: That changes the cases every run, which is why you lost this one.

feedback.correct: Same seed, same cases, same failure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the seed fixes.

explain.text: `random.Random(4)` produces the same sequence every run. That is why the stress loop takes a seed.

quiz.prose: The buggy fast count uses `<` for `<=`. The case is `xs = [2, 3, 3]`, $k = 6$.
quiz.question: What does the buggy fast count return?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the three pairs and their sums.

byKey.right: 3 is the correct count. The buggy one drops $3 + 3 = 6$, since $6 < 6$ is false.
byKey.none: Both pairs that sum to 5 are less than 6, so the buggy count still finds them.

explain.text: The pairs sum to 5, 5 and 6. The `<` version counts the two 5s and misses the 6. That one tie is the whole bug.

quiz.prose: A problem asks for any index $i$ with $a_i$ equal to the maximum. Your fast program prints 4 and the brute force prints 2 on `[1, 9, 3, 9]` (indices from 1).
quiz.question: What has the stress test found?

options.text: Nothing: both answers are valid, so compare with a checker
A bug in the fast program
options.why: You compared with equality. Index 4 also holds the maximum 9, so it is a valid answer.

options.text: A bug in the brute force
options.why: Index 2 holds 9 too. Both are right.

feedback.correct: Both 2 and 4 are valid; a checker would say so.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether each answer is valid.

explain.text: When several answers are allowed, a checker asks whether $a_{\text{answer}}$ is the maximum. Equality would raise false alarms on every tie.
